synthesis: Markets this week are being driven by one interlocking story: a hotter-than-expected core CPI print (+0.3% m/m) pushed the market-implied odds of a Fed rate hike at the Sept 15-16 FOMC from roughly 70% to 90%, sending the 10-year Treasury yield up 12bp to 4.95% — its highest level since 2023 and closing in on 2007 highs. Middle East tensions, including Iran's attacks on commercial and U.S. Navy vessels, are compounding the inflation picture by pushing WTI crude up 3.2% to $97. Credit markets aren't stressed — both IG and HY spreads tightened slightly on the week — and the VIX term structure remains in contango, meaning options markets aren't pricing panic despite small-caps (Russell 2000, -2.2% over 5 days) and the Dow (-2.1%) underperforming a Nasdaq held up by AI-infrastructure capex names. The FOMC decision on Sept 16 is the next clear catalyst for all of the above.

material_events.narrative: Broad-market and cyclical names have lagged over the past week as rising Treasury yields and oil prices weigh on rate-sensitive and industrial stocks more than mega-cap tech. A hot core CPI print (+0.3% m/m vs +0.2% forecast) raised the odds of a Fed hike at the Sept 15-16 FOMC meeting from ~70% to ~90%, and Iran's attacks on commercial/naval vessels in the Middle East have pushed oil higher, adding an inflation and cost headwind for industrials and consumer names that make up a larger share of the Dow than the Nasdaq.

material_events.narrative: Small caps are more rate-sensitive than large caps (higher average leverage, more floating-rate debt), so the run-up in the 10yr yield toward 5% on hot inflation data and hawkish Fed signaling has hit the Russell 2000 harder than large-cap indices over the past week. The same Middle East-driven oil spike also raises input costs disproportionately for smaller, less diversified companies.
